content: To improve the management of antiretroviral therapy (ART) patients, it is essential to streamline the tracking of individuals as they move through different points of contact within the healthcare system. However, as ART services are increasingly decentralized to primary healthcare settings, data systems must be adapted to accommodate limited local resources and staff capacity. In many cases, paper-based record-keeping continues to be used alongside electronic systems, which are typically reserved for higher-level data aggregation. The transfer of patients and their treatment records between facilities poses a significant challenge to effective clinical management and monitoring of ART retention. To address gaps in data, a unified system of unique patient identifiers and interoperable electronic patient monitoring systems across facilities is recommended. This approach is particularly critical as ART services expand to include facilities providing maternal and child health (MCH) care and tuberculosis (TB) services, and as patients requiring lifelong ART transition from these facilities to general HIV clinics. Retention and other treatment outcomes, such as viral suppression, mortality, and loss to follow-up, are typically measured among patient cohorts after specific durations on ART. Monitoring retention at 12 months is a standard practice recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), but additional assessments at 6, 24, 36, 48, and 60 months are also advised. Special studies are often required to investigate and estimate the true number of patients lost to follow-up, transferred to other sites, or deceased. For countries unable to report retention data from all ART sites, nationally representative estimates can be obtained by sampling a subset of clinics and patients using early warning indicator (EWI) methods or other surveillance protocols. Retention in treatment and adherence to ART regimens are critical not only for individual patient outcomes but also for preventing the development of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR). Surveillance of HIVDR in adults initiating ART or already receiving ART is essential to guide programmatic decisions. Adherence is commonly assessed through methods such as self-reported adherence, pill counts, and drug pick-up rates, each with its own strengths and limitations. While self-reported adherence and pill counts are easy to document, they often overestimate adherence. Drug pick-up rates, although not a direct measure of adherence, have been shown to correlate with viral suppression. High-quality ART patient management, including early treatment initiation, adherence to regimens, and retention in care, directly increases the likelihood of achieving viral suppression and avoiding drug resistance. Programs with high numbers of patients initiating ART with low CD4 counts should investigate the reasons for delayed treatment initiation. Late diagnosis, poor retention in pre-ART care, and inadequate referral systems may contribute to these delays, necessitating improvements in patient tracking systems. For pediatric and adolescent patients, care and treatment needs vary by age group. Early initiation of ART is a priority for infants and children under five years of age, while adolescents often experience higher rates of ART attrition and mortality. Monitoring systems must track children through the HIV care cascade as they transition from infancy to adulthood, ensuring continuity of care and treatment. Disaggregating ART data by age group can help monitor service quality and inform program planning and drug procurement. Among pregnant HIV-positive women, retention on ART is measured at 12 months after initiation, with earlier time points (e.g., 3, 6, 9 months) also considered to identify retention issues during the rollout of prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs. Disaggregating ART coverage and retention indicators by key populations is important to assess equity in service delivery. Surveys are often required to measure ART coverage and retention among key populations, as routine patient records may not include information identifying specific risk groups. For individuals co-infected with HIV and tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis B with severe chronic liver disease, the 2013 WHO guidelines recommend initiating ART regardless of CD4 count. This approach is critical for these populations, who are at higher risk of adverse outcomes if left untreated. Late ART initiation, defined as starting ART with a CD4 count ≤200 cells/mm³, is a significant risk factor for treatment failure and advanced disease progression. Programs should aim to reduce late initiation by addressing barriers to early diagnosis and treatment. Disaggregating data by priority populations can provide insights into equity in enrollment and inform strategies to improve access to care. Retention on ART is a key indicator of program success. It is measured as the number and percentage of people living with HIV who are alive and on ART at specific time points (e.g., 12, 24, 36 months) after initiation. High retention rates reflect effective program management and patient support systems. Where comprehensive data collection is not feasible, retention rates can be estimated from representative samples of ART clinics and patients.
